home-remodeling.local_heading: South Miami Houses, Inside and Out
intro_paragraphs: South Miami's housing stock tells the city's whole story: 1920s Tudor and Mediterranean cottages in Cambridge Lawns, postwar CBS ranches across Twin Lakes and Bird Road Estates, and larger new homes filling in the gaps between them. Most owners here never wanted a teardown. They bought for the canopy streets, the walk to Sunset Drive, and the lot their kids grew up on. What they want is the house brought up to the way they live now: open plans, a real primary suite, new systems behind the walls, and impact glass in every opening.

Remodeling here runs through the City of South Miami Building Department, a small municipal office with its own plan review and inspection staff, separate from the county system that governs High Pines and Ponce-Davis across Red Road. Exterior changes visible from the street can also require a pass before the city's Design Review Board — the panel longtime residents still call the ERPB — and homes inside the Cambridge Lawns Historic District answer to the Historic Preservation Board as well. None of it slows you down much when the drawings are complete and correct, which is exactly how we submit them.

South Florida has kept PGX Builders Group busy for more than 20 years: over 150 remodels and additions, every single one permitted and inspected. In South Miami, that experience looks like a fixed written scope before demolition starts, a supervisor on site every working day, finishes protected while the loud work happens, and one accountable team from first estimate to warranty. A remodel is a promise, and ours comes in writing.
home-remodeling.scope_heading: How Far a Whole-Home Remodel Goes
home-remodeling.scope_intro: One contract, one team, one schedule, from demolition through final inspection. A typical whole-home scope in South Miami includes:

scope_items.name: Layout and structural changes
scope_items.desc: Removing bearing walls in CBS ranches, adding engineered beams and columns, and reshaping choppy postwar floor plans into open living space that actually flows.

scope_items.name: Full MEP replacement
scope_items.desc: New electrical service, re-piped plumbing, and right-sized air conditioning for houses whose original systems date to the Eisenhower administration.

scope_items.name: Impact windows and doors
scope_items.desc: Miami-Dade approved impact glazing throughout, fitted to existing openings or enlarged ones, with HVHZ product approvals handled inside the permit package.

scope_items.name: Finishes and millwork
scope_items.desc: Stone, tile, wide-plank flooring, and built-in cabinetry installed under daily supervision, with everything that stays wrapped and protected from day one.

scope_items.name: Historic-sensitive exteriors
scope_items.desc: For Cambridge Lawns and other older streets, exterior work detailed to preserve the 1920s character the district was designated to protect.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel a home in South Miami?
faqs.a: Yes. Anything beyond paint and flooring — moving walls, changing plumbing or electrical, replacing windows — needs a permit from the City of South Miami Building Department, which runs its own plan review and inspections. Unpermitted work has a way of surfacing at sale or insurance time, and legalizing it after the fact costs more than doing it right once. We prepare the permit package, pull it under our license, and schedule every inspection.

faqs.q: How long does permitting take through the City of South Miami?
faqs.a: It depends on scope and on how complete the submittal is. A straightforward interior remodel moves faster than one involving structural changes or Design Review Board sign-off, which adds a board cycle. We won't promise a date a city department controls, but we control our end: complete drawings, engineering attached, and corrections answered quickly. We also sequence design and procurement so review time isn't wasted time.

faqs.q: My house is in Cambridge Lawns. Can I still remodel?
faqs.a: Yes. Cambridge Lawns was locally designated in 2005, so exterior changes get reviewed by the city's Historic Preservation Board with an eye toward the district's 1920s Tudor and Mediterranean character. Interior work is far more flexible. The process rewards good drawings and historically sensible details, both of which we bring. Plenty of homes in the district hide modern kitchens and brand-new systems behind their original facades.

faqs.q: Should I remodel or tear down and build new?
faqs.a: It comes down to the bones and the numbers. Many South Miami houses are solid concrete-block construction worth keeping, and a deep remodel, sometimes paired with an addition, often delivers the home you want without the cost and timeline of ground-up construction. When a teardown genuinely makes more sense, we'll tell you that too. We only win when the project is the right one.

faqs.q: What will a full remodel of my South Miami house cost?
faqs.a: The honest answer is a wide range, because scope drives everything: structural changes, full system replacement, and finish level each move the number significantly. We're a high-end contractor, not the low bid. What you're buying is engineering done right, a fixed written scope, and a schedule someone actually manages. After a walk-through we'll give you a realistic budget bracket before you spend anything on design.

kitchen-remodeling.title: Kitchen Remodeling for South Miami Homes | PGX Builders Group
kitchen-remodeling.meta_description: Kitchen remodeling in South Miami: custom cabinetry, stone islands, and engineered wall removals in CBS homes, permitted through the city. (786) 273-2524.
kitchen-remodeling.h1: A Kitchen Worthy of Sunset Drive
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom cabinetry, stone counters, and islands that anchor the whole house — designed, permitted through the City of South Miami, and built under daily supervision by a licensed general contractor.
intro_paragraphs: The postwar houses of University Gardens, Mango Terrace, and Cocoplum Terrace were drawn when the kitchen was a workroom: sealed off, single window, one circuit doing all the labor. That layout has aged worse than anything else in these houses. So South Miami owners open the wall to the dining room, land a stone island where it used to be, and build cabinetry to the ceiling — a kitchen that can host homework, cocktails, and Sunday dinner at once, a short walk from the downtown Sunset Drive restaurants it now competes with.

Even a kitchen that keeps its footprint touches plumbing, electrical, and mechanical work, which means a permit from the City of South Miami Building Department, a small office that still likes its application forms original and notarized. Take a wall out and you've added structural engineering, because in a concrete-block house that wall is usually doing something. Gas ranges need permitted fuel lines; induction usually needs a panel upgrade. We fold all of it into one submittal so the city reviews the project once, not piecemeal.

Kitchens are where sequencing separates contractors. Custom cabinetry has a lead time, stone gets templated only after the cabinets set, and a family can't live around an open trench forever. PGX runs kitchens on a fixed written scope and a schedule built backward from those realities, with a supervisor checking the site daily and the rest of your house sealed off and protected. One team owns it all — demolition, trades, millwork, punch list — from the first measurement to the last hinge adjustment.
kitchen-remodeling.scope_intro: Every kitchen is different, but the moving parts are consistent. Here's what PGX typically handles on a South Miami kitchen remodel:

scope_items.name: Custom cabinetry
scope_items.desc: Built-to-order boxes, inset or frameless fronts, and interiors planned around how you actually cook — installed level in houses where nothing else is.

scope_items.name: Stone counters and islands
scope_items.desc: Quartzite, marble, and granite templated after cabinet set, with seams placed deliberately and islands properly supported for the weight they carry.

scope_items.name: Structural wall removal
scope_items.desc: Engineered beams that open a closed 1960s plan to the dining and living rooms — calculated, permitted, and inspected rather than guessed at.

scope_items.name: Appliance and utility relocation
scope_items.desc: Moving ranges, sinks, and refrigeration means rerouting gas, water, and drains through a slab. We plan it before demolition, not after.

scope_items.name: Lighting and electrical
scope_items.desc: Layered task, ambient, and under-cabinet lighting on new circuits, replacing the single ceiling fixture the original builder considered sufficient.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a kitchen remodel in South Miami if no walls move?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. New circuits, a moved sink, a relocated gas line, or a rerouted vent all require permits from the City of South Miami Building Department even when the footprint stays put. Cabinet and counter swaps with zero trade work are the rare exception. Permits protect you at resale and insurance time, and inspections catch problems while they're still cheap to fix. We handle the paperwork and pull everything under our license.

faqs.q: How long does a South Miami kitchen remodel really take?
faqs.a: Longer than the TV version. Design and cabinet fabrication typically run a few months before demolition starts; construction itself is usually measured in weeks, driven by scope and inspection scheduling. The variable most people miss is lead time — cabinetry and stone set the calendar more than labor does. We won't demolish your kitchen until the long-lead items are ordered and the schedule is real.

faqs.q: Can you open the kitchen to the living room in a CBS house?
faqs.a: Almost always. In South Miami's concrete-block houses that wall is often carrying roof load, so the opening gets an engineered beam, proper bearing, and a city inspection — not just a sawzall and optimism. The result is the open plan these houses were never drawn with. We price the engineering into the scope up front so the structural work isn't a surprise change order.

faqs.q: Are custom cabinets worth it over stock?
faqs.a: For most of our clients, yes — but for specific reasons, not snobbery. Custom lets you use the full ceiling height, fit odd postwar dimensions without filler strips, and choose interiors that match how you cook. Stock and semi-custom make sense on some projects, and we'll say so when they do. What we won't do is build a high-end kitchen around boxes that fight the room.

faqs.q: Can we stay in the house during the remodel?
faqs.a: Most families do. We seal the work zone with dust barriers, keep protected paths for the crew, and help you set up a temporary kitchen — usually the old refrigerator, a microwave, and more patience than you expected. The honest part: there will be noisy days, and inspections dictate some of the calendar. Daily supervision keeps the disruption scheduled rather than random.

bathroom-remodeling.title: South Miami, FL Bathroom Remodeling | PGX Builders Group
bathroom-remodeling.meta_description: Bathroom remodeling in South Miami, FL. Primary suites, frameless showers, and waterproofing done right in postwar homes. Free walk-through: (786) 273-2524.
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Primary suites, frameless glass, and stone done properly, with the waterproofing membrane that never makes the photos. Licensed, insured, and permitted through the City of South Miami on every project.
intro_paragraphs: Walk into an untouched bathroom in Westerfield Manor or Pinecrest Villas and you'll usually find the 1958 original: pastel tile, a cast-iron tub, and five by eight feet of floor plan. South Miami owners have two moves. In the ranches, they combine a cramped bath and a closet into an actual primary suite with a frameless shower and real storage. On Manor Lane and the larger lots, it's the dated 1990s renovation being replaced with stone, a freestanding tub, and lighting that flatters instead of interrogates.

Bathrooms look small on a permit application and aren't. Moving fixtures means opening a slab; opening a slab in a 1950s house means meeting the cast-iron drains and galvanized supply lines hiding down there, and current code has opinions about both. Permits run through the City of South Miami Building Department, and the shower pan gets inspected before a single tile goes on — which is exactly the inspection you want passed. If a window sits in the wet area, it gets replaced with impact-rated, privacy-glazed product carrying a Miami-Dade approval.

The difference between a bathroom that photographs well and one that lasts is everything under the tile: slopes, membranes, flashing, fasteners rated for wet walls. That layer is where PGX spends its attention, because it's the layer you can't fix later without starting over. You get a fixed written scope, a supervisor on site daily, stone and glass measured by the people who install them, and the rest of the house protected from a very dusty little room. One team, one warranty, no finger-pointing between trades.
bathroom-remodeling.scope_intro: From gut demolition to the final bead of silicone, here's the work a South Miami bathroom remodel typically covers with PGX:

scope_items.name: Primary suite conversions
scope_items.desc: Combining a hallway bath, a closet, and wasted square footage into a suite the original floor plan never imagined it could hold.

scope_items.name: Frameless showers
scope_items.desc: Curbless entries and linear drains where the slab allows, full waterproofing membranes, and glass templated after tile so it actually fits.

scope_items.name: Freestanding tubs
scope_items.desc: Floor-mounted fillers mean plumbing routed through the slab — cut, roughed in, inspected, and poured back before the tub ever arrives.

scope_items.name: Stone and tile
scope_items.desc: Large-format porcelain, marble, and quartzite set flat and level, with niches and benches planned in the drawings, not improvised on site.

scope_items.name: Behind-the-wall upgrades
scope_items.desc: Replacing corroded cast-iron drains and narrowed galvanized supply lines while everything is open, so the new bathroom isn't plumbed like the old one.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel a bathroom in South Miami?
faqs.a: If plumbing or electrical work moves — and in a real remodel it almost always does — yes, through the City of South Miami Building Department. Inspections happen at stages you can't see afterward, like the shower pan and rough plumbing, which is precisely why they matter. Like-for-like fixture swaps are simpler, but few high-end projects stay that simple. We pull the permits and meet every inspector ourselves.

faqs.q: What will you find inside my 1950s walls?
faqs.a: In South Miami's postwar houses, typically cast-iron drains carrying decades of corrosion, galvanized supply lines that have narrowed with age, and framing details no current code would recognize. None of it is a crisis; all of it is best replaced while the walls are open. We assume some of this in the scope up front, so discoveries adjust the plan rather than detonate the budget.

faqs.q: How long does a bathroom remodel take?
faqs.a: For a full gut of a primary bath, think in terms of several weeks of construction after permits and materials are in hand — slab work, waterproofing cure times, and inspection scheduling all claim their days. What stretches timelines is starting before glass, stone, and fixtures are ordered, so we don't. You'll get a schedule tied to real lead times, not an optimistic guess.

faqs.q: Can two small bathrooms become one large one?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Adjacent postwar baths are one of the better remodeling opportunities in South Miami, since the plumbing is already concentrated in one place. Combining them takes structural review of what's between them, a drainage plan, and city permits, but the payoff is a primary bath that finally matches the caliber of the rest of your renovation. We'll tell you quickly whether your layout supports it.

faqs.q: What does a high-end bathroom remodel cost?
faqs.a: Ranges are wide and driven by three things: how far fixtures move, the stone and glass you select, and what we find in the walls. A faithful refresh costs a fraction of a full suite conversion with slab work. We're not the cheapest bid in Miami-Dade and don't try to be — the price buys waterproofing done correctly, a fixed scope, and one accountable team. Walk-throughs and estimates are free.

bathroom-remodeling.cta_sub: Show us the bathroom you've been tolerating. We'll walk the space, talk options, and put real numbers on it — in English o en español.

home-additions.title: Home Additions & Second Stories in South Miami | PGX Builders
home-additions.meta_description: Home additions in South Miami: rear extensions, second stories, and garage conversions permitted through the city Building Department. Call (786) 273-2524.
home-additions.h1: Your Lot Still Has Room Left
home-additions.hero_sub: Rear extensions, second stories, and in-law suites that make a 1950s South Miami cottage live like a new home — engineered, permitted through the city, and supervised every working day.
intro_paragraphs: South Miami real estate math is simple: the location, wedged between Coral Gables, Pinecrest, and the Metrorail, is superb, and the houses are smaller than the families in them. Across Red Road in High Pines and Ponce-Davis, the answer is usually a teardown. Inside the city, in Bird Road Estates, Cocoplum Terrace, and Twin Lakes, owners tend to keep the house and grow it instead: a rear extension into the deep lot, a second story over the original footprint, a garage turned into the office or suite the 1950s never planned for.

Additions live or die on the site plan. The City of South Miami's Land Development Code sets the setbacks and lot coverage that define your buildable envelope, the Building Department reviews the structural package, and exterior design can go before the city's Design Review Board. One local wrinkle worth respecting: any permit that requires a survey also requires a tree location plan from a licensed professional, because this city takes its canopy seriously. We confirm all of it — envelope, trees, board requirements — before you spend real money on design.

An addition is structural work first and architecture second, which is why PGX starts with the engineering: can the existing foundation and tie-beam carry a second story, or do they get upgraded before anything goes up? From there it's the discipline you'd expect from a contractor with 20-plus years in South Florida — a fixed written scope, daily supervision, new construction made weathertight fast, and the occupied half of your house kept livable and clean. When it's done, the addition should read as if the house was always this size.
home-additions.scope_heading: Five Ways South Miami Homes Grow
home-additions.scope_intro: Every addition starts with what the lot and the structure will allow. These are the projects we build most often here:

scope_items.name: Rear extensions
scope_items.desc: Living space extended toward the rear property line on engineered footings, the roof geometry worked out so the addition reads as original.

scope_items.name: Second-story additions
scope_items.desc: Doubling square footage without touching the setbacks — after an engineering assessment tells us what the original structure can honestly carry.

scope_items.name: Garage and carport conversions
scope_items.desc: Enclosed, insulated, conditioned, and legalized into offices, gyms, or guest rooms — permitted conversions, not the improvised kind these houses often hide.

scope_items.name: In-law and guest suites
scope_items.desc: Private quarters with their own entrance and bath, configured to what the city's zoning code allows on your particular lot.

scope_items.name: Tie-beam and foundation work
scope_items.desc: The unglamorous structural layer — new footings, reinforced tie-beams, upgraded connections — that lets a 1950s house safely hold a 2020s addition.

faqs.q: Can my South Miami house support a second story?
faqs.a: Many can, but nobody should answer that without an engineer looking at your foundation, walls, and tie-beam first. Plenty of the city's 1950s and 60s concrete-block houses were built stoutly enough to carry a second floor with targeted upgrades; some need new footings or reinforced columns; a few are better served by a rear extension. We start every second-story conversation with a structural assessment, not a sales pitch.

faqs.q: What setback and lot coverage rules apply to additions in South Miami?
faqs.a: They vary by zoning district under the City of South Miami's Land Development Code, and they determine how far back, how wide, and how tall you can build before design even begins. We verify your parcel's zoning, pull the actual numbers, and map the buildable envelope first — it's cheaper to learn the limits on paper than in a rejected permit. Exterior design may also need Design Review Board sign-off.

faqs.q: Will the city's tree rules affect my addition?
faqs.a: Quite possibly, and it's better to know early. South Miami requires a tree location plan, prepared by a licensed professional, with any permit that needs a survey, and removing protected canopy trees is its own regulated process. In practice we design footprints around significant oaks rather than through them — which usually produces a better addition anyway, since mature shade is half of what makes these lots valuable.

faqs.q: Should we add on or just move?
faqs.a: Run both numbers. Between transaction costs, financing, and what comparable larger homes nearby sell for, an addition often wins financially in South Miami — and it lets you keep the street, the schools, and the trees you actually chose. Sometimes moving genuinely is the better answer, and we've told clients so. Bring us your must-have list and we'll give you an honest read before you commit either way.

faqs.q: How disruptive is an addition while we live in the house?
faqs.a: Less than a whole-home remodel, more than a bathroom. Most of the heavy work happens outside the existing walls, and we keep the house sealed, secure, and weathertight at every stage — the connection between old and new gets opened as late in the schedule as possible. Expect noise during structural phases and a construction zone in the yard. Daily supervision keeps it orderly and predictable.

home-additions.cta_sub: Bring the wish list; we'll bring the tape measure and the zoning code. Site walk-throughs are free, in English o en español.

outdoor-living.title: Outdoor Living Construction, South Miami, FL | PGX Builders
outdoor-living.meta_description: Outdoor living in South Miami, FL. Covered terraces, summer kitchens, and pergolas engineered for hurricane wind, built around your oaks. (786) 273-2524.
outdoor-living.hero_sub: Terraces, summer kitchens, and pergolas built for South Miami's shade and its storms — anchored, drained, permitted through the city, and finished by one licensed, supervised crew.
outdoor-living.local_heading: The City of Pleasant Living, Outside
intro_paragraphs: South Miami calls itself the City of Pleasant Living, and the backyards make the argument: deep lots under mature oaks along Manor Lane and the streets south of Sunset Drive, shade you couldn't buy new at any price. Owners here are turning that shade into rooms — a covered terrace off the family room, a summer kitchen that handles Saturday properly, a driveway and entry that finally match the house behind them. Done right, the outdoor half of a South Miami home earns its keep nearly year-round.

Outdoor projects are still construction, and the City of South Miami treats them that way. Pergolas, summer kitchens, and driveways take permits through the city's Building Department; work visible from the street may also pass through the Design Review Board. Because all of Miami-Dade sits in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, anything anchored — a pergola, a fixed canopy, an outdoor structure — needs engineering and connections rated for real wind, not just something that looks sturdy at the garden center. Gas and electric to a summer kitchen get inspected like the indoor kind, because they are.

PGX builds exteriors as one coordinated package instead of five overlapping subcontracts. Re-roof, stucco, paint, impact openings, terrace, and driveway get sequenced in the order that protects each finished layer — nobody drags a compressor across your new pavers in month three. You get a fixed written scope, a supervisor on site daily, root zones and landscaping protected while we work, and a single team accountable from the first drawing to the final walkthrough. It's the difference between a yard that got projects and a home that got finished.
outdoor-living.scope_intro: From the roofline to the property line, this is the exterior work PGX takes on across South Miami:

scope_items.name: Covered terraces
scope_items.desc: Roofed outdoor rooms tied properly into the existing structure, with fans, lighting, and drainage designed in from the very start.

scope_items.name: Summer kitchens
scope_items.desc: Grills, gas, refrigeration, and stone counters built on permitted utility runs, with materials chosen to shrug off Miami humidity.

scope_items.name: Pergolas and shade structures
scope_items.desc: Engineered for hurricane-zone wind loads and anchored to real footings — the version that's still standing the morning after a storm.

scope_items.name: Driveways and hardscape
scope_items.desc: Pavers and concrete graded to move water away from the house, laid out around root zones instead of over them.

scope_items.name: Exterior envelope package
scope_items.desc: Stucco repair, paint, impact windows and doors, and re-roof coordination handled as one sequenced project under one contract and warranty.

faqs.q: Are permits required for pergolas and summer kitchens in South Miami?
faqs.a: Yes, in nearly every case. Structures, roofed areas, gas lines, electrical circuits, and most driveway work all require permits from the City of South Miami Building Department, and anchored structures need wind-load engineering because the whole county is a High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. It's more process than a weekend project deserves — which is a good clue these shouldn't be weekend projects. We handle design, permits, and inspections as one scope.

faqs.q: Can you build a terrace without hurting our oak trees?
faqs.a: That's the assignment on most South Miami lots, and yes. The city requires a professional tree location plan with survey-based permits and guards its canopy closely, so we design terraces and driveways around root zones, keep excavation away from critical roots, and fence off trees during construction. The mature shade is why your backyard is worth building in — we treat it as part of the structure.

faqs.q: What materials actually survive outdoors in Miami?
faqs.a: Fewer than the showrooms suggest. Marine-grade stainless for kitchen components, dense stone or porcelain for counters and floors, teak or marine-grade polymer for cabinetry — and hardware and fasteners matter as much as surfaces. Humidity, UV, and summer rain destroy anything borrowed from an indoor spec sheet. We've spent 20-plus years watching South Florida weather test materials, and we only install the ones that pass.

faqs.q: Does exterior work need Design Review Board approval in South Miami?
faqs.a: Some of it does. The city's Design Review Board looks at certain exterior changes visible from the street, and its sign-off comes before the permit. It's an added step, not an obstacle: complete drawings and sensible design move through cleanly, and we prepare the presentation package and attend so you don't have to. Backyard work on an interior lot is typically the simpler path.

faqs.q: When is the best time of year to build outdoors?
faqs.a: We build year-round; South Florida just makes you schedule differently. Summer afternoons bring rain, so concrete pours and roofing happen in morning windows, and hurricane season means sites stay secured and materials strapped or stored. The practical advice: start design and permitting a season before you want to be grilling, because the paperwork doesn't care about the weather.
